title: Why Are My Energy Bills So High? HVAC Causes
h1: Why Are My Energy Bills So High? Signs Your HVAC System Is to Blame
description: High energy bills often trace back to the HVAC system. Learn the warning signs of an inefficient system, the common causes, and what you can fix yourself.
quick_answer: Rising energy bills usually come from an HVAC system working harder than it should. Common causes are dirty filters and coils, leaky or poorly insulated ducts, low refrigerant, thermostat problems, an aging or wrongly sized system, and missed maintenance. Weather and rate changes play a part too, so compare usage, not just the dollar amount.
body:
Is it the HVAC system or something else?

Before blaming the system, look at your bill's usage, measured in kilowatt-hours for electricity and therms for gas. Utility rates change, and heat waves or a cold snap raise everyone's usage. Compare this month to the same month last year. If usage is up noticeably in similar weather, the HVAC system is a likely suspect, since heating and cooling are usually the biggest energy users in a home.

Also look at when the jump started. A sudden rise often lines up with a specific change, like a part failing, a duct coming loose in the attic, or a thermostat that reset itself after a power outage. A slow climb over a few years is more typical of an aging system, dirty coils or gradually worsening duct leaks.

Other things that can raise bills include a pool pump, a second refrigerator, an electric vehicle, or a new household member working from home.

What are the signs of an inefficient HVAC system?

  • Longer run times. The system runs and runs but struggles to reach the setpoint.
  • Short cycling. It turns on and off every few minutes.
  • Uneven temperatures between rooms or floors.
  • Weak airflow from the vents.
  • Warm air in cooling mode, or air that never feels quite cold enough.
  • More dust and a stuffy feel in the house.
  • New noises like buzzing, rattling or grinding.
  • Frequent repairs in the last few years.

What causes an HVAC system to use more energy?

Dirty filters and coils. A clogged filter chokes airflow. Dirty indoor and outdoor coils can't move heat well, so the system runs longer. Coastal salt air and inland dust both build up on outdoor coils.

Leaky ducts. In many local homes, ducts run through the attic, which can get extremely hot in summer. Leaks and thin insulation waste cooled or heated air before it reaches the rooms.

Low refrigerant. Refrigerant doesn't get used up, so low levels mean a leak. The system loses capacity and runs longer to keep up.

Thermostat issues. A thermostat in direct sun, near a kitchen or poorly programmed can keep the system running when it doesn't need to.

Wrong size. An oversized system short cycles and an undersized one runs nonstop. Both waste energy.

Age. Older equipment loses efficiency over time, and units from a couple of decades ago are much less efficient than today's systems to begin with.

What can I fix myself?

  1. Change the air filter and set a reminder for the next one.
  2. Clear the outdoor unit. Trim plants back about two feet and gently rinse the coil with a hose.
  3. Open and clear vents that are blocked by furniture or rugs.
  4. Program the thermostat to ease off when you're asleep or away. Check that the schedule still matches your routine, since many are set once and forgotten.
  5. Close blinds on sun-facing windows during hot afternoons, especially west-facing rooms in inland homes.
  6. Check the attic hatch and weatherstripping on exterior doors. A loose hatch lets hot attic air spill into the hallway all summer.

When should I call a technician?

If bills stay high after the basics, a tune-up is the next step. A technician can clean the coils, check refrigerant levels and electrical parts, measure airflow, and inspect the ducts for leaks. Those are the problems homeowners can't see or fix on their own, and they often have the biggest impact on energy use.

It also helps to bring a few recent bills to the conversation. Seeing when usage rose, and by how much, gives the technician clues about where to look first, whether it's the cooling side in summer or the furnace in winter.

If the system is older and needs frequent repairs, it may be time to compare repair costs with a more efficient replacement. Our HVAC team can inspect your system and explain your options, and our duct sealing and repair service tackles one of the most common hidden energy wasters.
faqs: Why is my electric bill so high in summer?

Air conditioning is usually the biggest summer energy user, especially in hot inland areas. A dirty filter or coil, leaky attic ducts, low refrigerant or an aging AC can all push usage higher than it should be.
Does a dirty air filter really raise energy bills?
Yes. A clogged filter restricts airflow, so the system runs longer to heat or cool the house. It can also cause a frozen coil or overheating that leads to repairs.
Should I turn my AC off when I leave the house?

Setting it higher while you are out usually saves more than leaving it at a cool setting, and it avoids forcing the system to recover from a very hot house. A programmable or smart thermostat makes this automatic.
Can leaky ducts raise my energy bill?

Yes. Ducts that leak into a hot attic or garage waste heated and cooled air before it reaches your rooms, making the system run longer. Sealing and insulating them often improves comfort and efficiency.
